note 4 overlapping conductor shape(s) were merged into 2 — copper that overlaps on one level is one conductor, in 3D as in the planar model.
note Port 1 ('1') at (0, 0 µm) was taken to be on the conductor's low-x (left) end (inferred from the nearest conductor boundary) of level 0 ('M1'), driving current in the +x direction, at 50 Ω.
note Port 2 ('2') at (2300, 0 µm) was taken to be on the conductor's high-x (right) end (inferred from the nearest conductor boundary) of level 1 ('M2'), driving current in the −x direction, at 50 Ω.
note Port 1 at its line's end is a vertical lumped sheet 200 µm wide and 100 µm tall from 'M1' down to 'Ground' (the air box's floor): as this setup names.
note Port 2 at its line's end is a vertical lumped sheet 200 µm wide and 305 µm tall from 'M2' down to 'Ground' (the air box's floor): as this setup names.
note 'M1', 'M2', 'Via' name no material, so their σ is a number of unknown temperature and is used as given at 20 °C. Name a material with an α₂₀ to have it evaluated at the operating temperature.
note The air box's floor is 'Ground' as a PEC plane at 5 µm: it is the lowest ground-reference conductor, nothing is drawn on it and nothing is drawn below it.
note 'M1/1' and 1 other conductor(s) are under 3 skin depths thick at 1 GHz, so Thin Metal Correction gives the faces that thickness (4.87 µm on 'M1/1'). Its resistance levels off at the DC value. Near two to three skin depths a line can still read up to 25 % low. A wide line close to ground can read high, because its faces carry unequal current: up to 20 % on a line 5 times wider than its height over ground, and 50 % at 50 times.
